436.content: In each `Result` that `Results()` delivers for an `AddAll` group on a result worker, in its `JobId` field. See adding many jobs.

437.content: It is the empty string when the job has no ID.

438.content: An in-memory queue keeps at most one job per given ID in the queue. While a job with an ID is in the queue, the queue refuses a second `Add` with the same ID. That `Add` returns a `nil` handle and `false`.

439.content: The worker below is created with `WithAutoRun(false)`, so the jobs wait in the queue until `Start`. On a running worker, the first job could leave the queue before the second `Add`, which releases its ID and lets the second one in.

440.content: The second `Add` with the ID `refresh` is refused and returns no handle, so `refresh 2` never runs. The `AddAll` item is accepted, because its ID is `g:refresh`. Once the jobs have left the queue, `refresh` can be used again.

441.content: That suits work where many callers ask for the same thing, and one waiting job is enough.

442.content: The queue holds an ID while its job is in the queue. The ID is released when a worker takes the job out of the queue, or when `Purge` removes it.

443.content: A worker takes jobs out of the queue before it runs them. With a FIFO queue, it may take several at once in a batch (how it works). A job in a batch, or one parked by a pause or stop, has left the queue, so it has released its ID. Its status still reads `Queued`. A duplicate `Add` is accepted at that point.

444.content: So the rule is one job per ID *in the queue*, not one live job per ID. It does not stop the same ID from running twice at once: when a worker has taken the first job, the ID is free.

445.content: Closing a job with its handle's `Close` does not free its ID. `Close` leaves the job in the queue, so it keeps the ID until the worker reaches it or `Purge` removes it. See closing a queued job.

446.content: Only IDs you gave, with `WithJobId` or `Item.ID`. A generated ID is not checked, and two jobs with no ID are both stored.

447.content: `AddAll` applies the same rule per item. `AddAll` skips an item whose ID belongs to a job in the queue. It also skips a repeat within the same slice while the first copy is still in the queue. A running worker may already have taken that first copy. Items get a `g:` prefix, so an item with ID `a` and an `Add` with `WithJobId("a")` do not collide.

448.content: Every in-memory queue is checked: FIFO and priority queues, and their error and result variants.

449.content: A queue you bind with `WithQueue` or `WithPriorityQueue` is checked only if it implements `IDedupQueue` or `IDedupPriorityQueue`. Without that, the queue stores the duplicate.

450.content: `Add` also returns `false` for a full queue and for a closed one, and it does not say which of the three it was. See queues.

451.content: Persistent and distributed queues do not work this way. Storage that implements `IDedupQueue` keeps an ID for a window that the storage itself sets. `Add` returns `true` for a repeat, but the storage keeps the job only once. IDs there must be unique across everything you add. Use something like a UUID, not a counter that restarts. The `IDedupQueue` documentation has the details.

453.content: Read the four counters of a worker, and what each one counts.

457.content: When the equation does not hold

460.content: Every worker keeps four counters over its lifetime. `Metrics()` returns them. They tell you how much work the worker has taken in and how it went, without tracking jobs yourself.

461.content: This page covers workers bound to in-memory queues. For persistent and distributed queues, see persistence.

462.content: `Metrics` has four read methods, each returning a `uint64`:

463.content:
| Method        | Counts                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Submitted()` | jobs the queue accepted. One for each `Add` that returns `true`, and one for each item of `AddAll` the queue took. An `Add` that returns `false` adds nothing. |

464.content:
| Method        | Counts                                                            |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Completed()` | jobs whose function has returned, whether it succeeded or failed. |

465.content:
| Method         | Counts                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Successful()` | jobs whose function returned without an error and without a panic. A plain worker's function has no error to return, so for it this means it returned normally. |

466.content:
| Method     | Counts                                              |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `Failed()` | jobs whose function returned an error, or panicked. |

467.content: A job that runs counts once in `Completed` and once in `Successful` or `Failed`. After a worker has gone idle, `Completed` equals `Successful` plus `Failed`, unless you called `Reset` partway.

468.content: A job that never runs counts in `Submitted` and in none of the others. That happens to a job that is closed before it starts: closed through its handle, or removed by `Purge`. It also happens to a topic payload that is dropped unread, as below. Only a job that ran increments `Completed`.

469.content: A topic counts too: each `Publish` adds one to `Submitted` of every worker subscribed to it at that moment. The subscriber's worker turns a payload into a job only when it takes the payload. So an unread payload is counted as submitted, but it is not a job yet. Unsubscribing drops such payloads.

470.content: The program below adds three jobs to an error worker. Job 2 returns an error. It waits until the worker is idle and reads the four counters.

471.content: All three jobs were submitted and completed. Two succeeded, and job 2 is the one failed job, so `Completed` equals `Successful` plus `Failed`.

472.content: **The counters are cumulative.** They start at zero when the worker is created, and nothing but `Reset` clears them. Pausing, stopping, restarting and purging do not change them.

473.content: **They are safe to read from any goroutine.** Each method is one atomic read.

474.content: **Four reads are not one snapshot.** A job can finish between two of them. So four values read while jobs run can be off by as many jobs as finish between the reads.

475.content: **A job's own `Wait` can return a moment before `Completed` counts it.** The worker closes a finished job, which releases `Wait`. Just after that, the worker counts the job as completed. `Successful` and `Failed` are already counted by then. To read settled values, wait for the worker with `WaitUntilIdle` or `Wait` first. Waiting compares them.

476.content: On a worker with no job waiting or running, `Submitted == Completed`. Three things break this: a job that was closed before it ran, storage shared with another worker, and a `Reset` partway. A closed job is the most common case: you purged it, closed it through its handle, or a topic dropped it unread.

477.content: The rule comes from a general equation. A job is waiting, running or done, so for a worker with nothing running you might expect:

478.content: `NumPending` is the jobs that have not started, plus the finished jobs of a batch that has not ended. `NumProcessing` is the jobs running right now, counted as busy goroutines. With no job waiting or running, both are 0, so the equation becomes `Submitted == Completed`.

479.content: The equation does not hold in these cases:

480.content: **A job closed before it ran breaks it.** `Purge`, and closing a queued job through its handle, leave `Submitted` higher than the sum. Such a job was counted when it was added, and it never reaches `Completed`, because only a job that ran does. Once the worker has dropped it, it is not pending either, so nothing on the right counts it. A job closed through its handle still counts in `NumPending` until the worker reaches it, so the gap opens then.

481.content: **While jobs run, the sum can be too high.** A goroutine can take several jobs from an in-memory FIFO queue or a topic into a batch (batched dispatch). `NumProcessing` counts that goroutine as one. `NumPending` keeps counting the finished jobs of the batch until the whole batch has ended. But `Completed` counts each job as it finishes. For that time the sum can run above `Submitted`.

482.content: **Unsubscribing with unread payloads breaks it.** `Unsubscribe`, `Close` on the subscription, and `Close` on the topic all end a subscription. They drop the payloads it has not read. `Publish` counted them in `Submitted`. They never run, so they never reach `Completed`. The worker no longer counts them as pending, because their subscription is gone. `Purge` on a subscription drops the unread payloads the same way.

483.content: **Storage shared between workers breaks it.** `Add` counts in `Submitted` on the worker whose handle you call. The worker that takes the job counts it in `Completed`. A queue you wrote and bound to two workers with `WithQueue` splits the counters between them, so the equation holds for neither.

484.content: **`Reset` breaks it.** It zeroes `Submitted` and `Completed`. The jobs still waiting or running count on the right side of the equation, and no longer on the left.

485.content: So use the equation on a worker with nothing running, where none of these cases applies. If `Submitted == Completed` does not hold on a worker with no job waiting or running, look at the cases above first. Do not use the equation as a live check while jobs run.

486.content: The program below checks the equation on an idle worker, then on a worker paused with `PauseAndWait` with two jobs waiting, then after `Purge`.

487.content: The equation holds on the idle worker: 1 = 0 + 0 + 1. It also holds on the paused one: 3 = 2 + 0 + 1. A paused worker starts nothing, and its two jobs wait in the queue. After `Purge` the right side is 1 and `Submitted` is still 3: the two purged jobs never ran, so they never reach `Completed`.

488.content: `Reset` sets all four counters to zero. It does not touch the queue or the jobs that are running.

489.content: The four counters are cleared one after another, not in one step.

490.content: A job that was waiting or running when you call it is counted in `Completed` when it finishes, though its `Submitted` is gone. After a `Reset` in the middle of a run, `Completed` can be higher than `Submitted`.

491.content: Call `Reset` when the worker is idle, as the program below does.

492.content: Both jobs ran before the `Reset`, so the counters read 2 before it and 0 after.

493.content: A named worker's counters are also what the REST handler reports, and the Prometheus example exports the same four. See REST API and Prometheus.

495.content: FIFO and priority queues, how to bound one with a capacity, what Add returns when a queue is full, and Len, Purge and Close.

500.content: Workers and queues showed how a worker gets a queue. This page covers the in-memory queues: the first-in first-out queue and the priority queue. It shows how to bound them, and the calls that inspect and empty them.

501.content:
| Method      | Binds                      | Jobs leave in             |
| ----------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `BindQueue` | a first-in first-out queue | the order they were added |

502.content:
| Method              | Binds            | Jobs leave in  |
| ------------------- | ---------------- | -------------- |
| `BindPriorityQueue` | a priority queue | priority order |

503.content: `Add` on a FIFO queue takes the data. `Add` on a priority queue takes the data and then an `int` priority:

504.content: The worker is created with `WithAutoRun(false)`, so all three jobs wait until `Start`. `alert` runs first although it was added second, and `report` runs before `digest` because they share a priority and `report` was added first.

505.content: Each queue below has its own worker. Add jobs to both queues, then start the workers. The rail shows the order the jobs leave in.

506.content: **A lower number runs first.** Among the jobs that are waiting, priority 1 goes before priority 10, whatever order they were added in. Priorities can be negative. Jobs with the same priority run in the order they were added.

507.content: **Priority orders waiting jobs only.** A job that is already running is not interrupted. A worker takes one job at a time from a priority queue. So a high-priority job added later does not wait behind jobs already handed out in a batch. How it works explains batches.

508.content: An `Item` in `AddAll` carries its own priority. See adding many jobs.

509.content: A job's priority is not the same as `WithQueuePriority`. That option ranks whole queues against each other when several are bound to one worker. Strategies covers it.

510.content: A queue has no limit unless you set one. `WithQueueCapacity` bounds how many jobs can wait in it. Pass it when you bind the queue. A value below 1 means no limit.

511.content: When the queue is full, `Add` does not block. It returns a `nil` handle and `false`. Treat that as backpressure: retry later, drop the job, or tell your caller to slow down. A full queue, a closed queue and a duplicate job ID all give the same `false`. `IsFull()` tells you whether the queue is at its capacity.

512.content: Two jobs fit, and `Add` refuses the third with a `nil` handle. The worker is not started, so nothing leaves the queue to make room. Without `WithAutoRun(false)` the worker would take the first jobs at once and the queue would have room again.

513.content: Set a capacity below and add jobs until the queue refuses one. Then start the worker: it takes the waiting jobs into a batch, and the queue has room again. `Purge()` and `Close()` are covered in the next section.

514.content: Capacity bounds the jobs still in the queue. On a FIFO queue, a worker can take several jobs into a batch. Those jobs are no longer in the queue. So in total, more jobs than the capacity can wait. A priority queue is not batched. See what batching means for your code.

515.content: If you bind your own queue, the capacity reaches it only when it implements `CapacitySetter`, and only then does the queue refuse jobs. Without it, `Add` keeps accepting jobs, although `IsFull()` still compares `Len()` with the number you passed.

516.content: These three work on the queue handle that `Bind...` returns.

517.content: **`Len()`** is the number of jobs waiting in the queue.

518.content: It leaves out a job a worker has taken into a batch, and a job the worker parked when you paused or stopped it. The worker's `NumPending` counts those.

519.content: A job you closed while it waited still counts until the worker reaches it. See closing a queued job.

520.content: The queue handle also has a `NumPending` method. It is deprecated: use `Len`.

521.content: **`Purge()`** removes every job that has not started and closes each one.

522.content: A purged job's `Status()` reads `Closed`, `Wait` returns, `Err` returns `nil` and `Result` returns the zero value.

523.content: Jobs a worker had already taken into a batch, or parked, are closed too. The worker closes a batched job as it reaches it.

524.content: A job that is running is not affected.

525.content: Purging also frees the IDs of the jobs it removes.

526.content: **`Close()`** stops the queue taking jobs: every later `Add` returns `false`. With the built-in queues, jobs already in the queue stay there and still run. The queue stays closed, and VarMQ has no call to reopen it. The worker is not stopped, and neither are other queues bound to it. For the worker, see the lifecycle. The built-in queues return a `nil` error from `Close`.

527.content: `Purge` empties the queue and closes both jobs, so their status reads `Closed`. After `Close`, `Add` refuses `d`, but `c`, added before the queue closed, still runs once the worker starts.

528.content: `WithQueue` and `WithPriorityQueue` bind a queue you wrote, instead of an in-memory one. It has to implement `IQueue` or `IPriorityQueue`.

529.content: The worker calls `Enqueue` when you call `Add`, and `Dequeue` when it has a free slot. The items are the jobs themselves, so store them and return them unchanged. `Purge` uses `Values` to find the jobs to close, so `Values` has to return what is in the queue.

530.content: The worker batches a queue passed to `WithQueue` like the built-in FIFO queue, so it can take several jobs at once. The exception is a queue that also implements `IAcknowledgeable`. A queue passed to `WithPriorityQueue` is handled like the built-in priority queue, one job at a time.

531.content: Two optional interfaces add behaviour: `CapacitySetter`, above, for `WithQueueCapacity`, and `IDedupQueue` with `IDedupPriorityQueue` for job ID checks. Adapters lists every queue interface. For queues that survive a restart or are shared between processes, see persistence.

533.content: How a worker with several queues picks the next job: the Priority, RoundRobin, MaxLen and MinLen strategies.

538.content: What priority does under the other strategies

539.content: A worker can have several **sources** bound to it. A source is a queue, a priority queue or a topic subscription. When a slot becomes free, the worker needs a rule for which source gives the next job. That rule is the **strategy**. Workers and queues introduced it; this page covers all four.

540.content: Each source has a **rank**: the number you set with `WithQueuePriority` or `WithTopicPriority`. A lower rank goes first. **The list** is every source ordered by rank, lowest first, and by bind order among equal ranks. Every strategy walks the list in that order.

541.content: `Strategy` has four values. `WithStrategy` sets one when you create the worker, and `DefaultStrategy` changes the default for workers created after the call.

542.content:
| Strategy                | Takes the next job from                                | Ties                   |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| `Priority`, the default | the source with the lowest rank that has a waiting job | the source bound first |

543.content:
| Strategy     | Takes the next job from                        | Ties                           |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `RoundRobin` | the next source in turn that has a waiting job | not applicable: it takes turns |

544.content:
| Strategy | Takes the next job from               | Ties                                    |
| -------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `MaxLen` | the source with the most waiting jobs | the source that comes first in the list |

545.content:
| Strategy | Takes the next job from                                         | Ties                                    |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `MinLen` | the source with the fewest waiting jobs, ignoring empty sources | the source that comes first in the list |

546.content: Pick a strategy below and take jobs one at a time. The queues start with 2 alerts, 1 report and 3 emails, the same as the RoundRobin and length programs below. Before each job, the scene says which queue the strategy chooses and why. Picking another strategy starts a new worker, because a worker keeps its strategy.

547.content: A few rules hold for all four:

548.content: **Empty sources are skipped.** A strategy only chooses among sources that have a job waiting.

549.content: **The strategy is fixed when the worker is created.** There is no call to change it later.

550.content: **It decides every job.** With two or more sources bound, the worker hands out one job at a time. It picks the source again each time, from the source lengths at that moment. How it works explains why it does not batch in this case. With a single source there is nothing to choose.

551.content: **The zero value of `Strategy` is `RoundRobin`, not the default.** A worker created without `WithStrategy` uses `Priority`.

552.content: `WithQueuePriority` sets the rank of a queue when you bind it. It works on `BindQueue` and `BindPriorityQueue`. The programs on this page use a worker with concurrency 1 and `WithAutoRun(false)`. No job starts until every queue is filled, and the worker takes one job at a time. So the jobs print in the order the worker took them.

553.content: The emails were added first but run last. Both alerts go before the report, and the report before the emails.

554.content: **A lower rank goes first.** The worker takes from the first source in the list that has a job waiting. A source with no rank set gets the largest possible rank, `math.MaxInt`, so it comes after every source that has a smaller one. Sources with the same rank go in the order they were bound.

555.content: Priority does not share. While a source with a lower rank has jobs waiting, a source with a higher rank gets none. A busy `alerts` queue can keep `emails` waiting.

556.content: A topic subscription is in the same list. `WithTopicPriority` sets its rank like `WithQueuePriority` does. See topics.

557.content: This is the rank of a whole source. It is not the priority you pass to `Add` on a priority queue, which orders the jobs inside that one queue. See queues.

558.content: The worker goes through the list one source per job, then starts over. It skips a source that is empty when its turn comes, so once a source is empty, the others share the turns.

559.content: One job from each queue in turn. `reports` is empty after its first job, so the later turns go to `alerts` and `emails`.

560.content: Both compare how many jobs are waiting in each source, read again for every job.

561.content: **`MaxLen`** takes from the longest source. Each job it takes makes that source shorter. While nothing new arrives, the turns pass to the next-longest source. So the longest sources get shorter together.

562.content: **`MinLen`** takes from the shortest source that is not empty. It runs a short source to empty, then moves to the next shortest. A long source waits while any shorter source still has jobs.

563.content: On a tie, both take the source that comes first in the list.

564.content: The queues start with 2 alerts, 1 report and 3 emails. `MaxLen` takes an email from the longest queue, then breaks the 2-2 tie with `alerts`, which comes first in the list. When `reports` and `emails` tie at 1 each, `reports` goes first, so an email runs last. `MinLen` empties `reports`, then `alerts`, and leaves the long `emails` queue for last.

565.content: "In order" here means the order the jobs leave the queues. With a concurrency above 1 several of them run at once, and their output can interleave.

566.content: `RoundRobin`, `MaxLen` and `MinLen` do not choose by rank. They still go through the list in rank order. So a rank sets the order of the `RoundRobin` turns. It also sets which source wins a tie in `MaxLen` and `MinLen`. If you give no ranks, the list is the bind order.

568.content: Publish once, and every subscribed worker gets its own job. Topics are in-memory only.

575.content: A queue gives each job to one worker. A `Topic` gives each payload to every worker subscribed to it. Use one when several workers must each act on the same event, such as sending an email and updating stock for the same order.

576.content:
|                | In-memory queue  | Topic                                          |
| -------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Who gets a job | one worker, once | every subscribed worker, each with its own job |

577.content:
|               | In-memory queue | Topic              |
| ------------- | --------------- | ------------------ |
| You send with | `queue.Add(x)`  | `topic.Publish(x)` |

578.content:
|              | In-memory queue           | Topic    |
| ------------ | ------------------------- | -------- |
| You get back | a job handle and a `bool` | a `bool` |

579.content: **Topics are in-memory only.** A topic lives in your process. Nothing is written to disk, and a payload is lost when the process exits.

580.content: `NewTopic` creates a topic for payloads of one type. `WithTopic` subscribes a worker to it:

581.content: Each worker prints all four orders. The stock lines come first because its jobs are shorter, and with concurrency 2 two of them can print in either order.

582.content: `WithTopic` is available on the worker that `NewWorker` returns. Error and result workers cannot subscribe: see the table in worker types.

583.content: `WithTopic` returns a `Subscription`, the worker's handle on the topic. A subscription has no `Add`, because the topic is the only producer. Two calls panic: subscribing a worker to a topic it is already subscribed to, and passing a `nil` topic. A worker can subscribe again after it unsubscribes.

584.content: `Publish` stores the payload once and wakes every subscribed worker. Each worker then makes its own job from the payload. The payload is copied by value, so if `T` is a pointer or holds pointers, maps or slices, every subscriber shares what they point to.

585.content: `Publish` returns `true` once the payload is stored. It returns `false`, and no subscriber gets the payload, in three cases:

586.content: no worker is subscribed, so the payload has nowhere to go;

588.content: the topic is full: see capacity.

589.content: It returns when the payload is stored, not when the jobs finish. To wait for a subscriber's jobs, wait on that subscriber's worker: waiting covers how. A job made from a payload gets its ID from the subscriber's own job ID generator, and a worker with no generator gives it none.

590.content: A worker receives only the payloads published after it subscribed. A payload that `Publish` refused for lack of subscribers is not kept for the next one.

591.content: `Publish` refuses payload 1 because nobody is subscribed, and that payload is gone. The `email` worker subscribes before payload 2 and gets 2 and 3. The `audit` worker subscribes after payload 2, so it gets only 3.

592.content: A topic keeps one copy of each payload in a shared in-memory log, however many workers subscribe. Each subscription reads the log at its own position, so a slow worker does not block `Publish` or the other workers. A payload is freed once every subscription has read it. In the diagram, that is why a chunk of the log stays while the slower worker's cursor is still on it.

593.content: So a subscriber that is slow, paused or stopped keeps every payload that it has not read. It keeps them until it reads them all, purges or unsubscribes. For a worker that may stall, set a capacity.

594.content: `Unsubscribe` on the subscription ends it. The worker gets nothing more from the topic, and the payloads it has not read yet are dropped. A job the worker has already taken from the topic is not recalled. A running job finishes, and a job waiting in a batch still runs. Calling it twice is safe. `Close` on the subscription does the same.

595.content: `Purge` on a subscription keeps the subscription and drops the unread payloads. Unlike `Unsubscribe`, it also discards the jobs the worker has taken from the topic but not started. So a job waiting in a batch does not run. A job that is already running finishes. `Purge` does not call `Close` on the payloads. `Len` is the number of payloads the subscription has not read, and `Worker()` returns its worker.

596.content: To end every subscription at once, call `Close` on the topic. It unsubscribes all of them, and every later `Publish` returns `false`. `NumSubscribers()` tells you how many are attached.

597.content: Both workers get payload 1. After the stock subscription ends, one subscriber is left, and payload 2 goes only to `email`.

598.content: A topic has no limit unless you set one. `WithTopicCapacity` bounds it when you create it.

599.content: The limit applies to the slowest subscription. Once it has that many payloads unread, `Publish` returns `false`, the way `Add` does on a full queue, and the refused payload reaches no subscriber. Room comes back as that subscription reads, purges or unsubscribes. A value below 1 means no limit.

600.content: The worker is created with `WithAutoRun(false)`, so it reads nothing until `Start`. Two payloads fit, and the third is refused while 2 are unread. Once the worker has read both, there is room, and the same `Publish` succeeds.

601.content: `IsFull()` on the topic tells you whether it is at its capacity right now, and the answer can change right after. On a subscription, `IsFull()` is true when that subscription is at the capacity, which makes it the one refusing `Publish`. Act on the result of `Publish` itself, not on `IsFull`.

602.content: A topic subscription is one more source of its worker, next to any queues bound to it. The worker's strategy picks which source gives the next job. `WithTopicPriority` ranks the subscription the way `WithQueuePriority` ranks a queue: a lower number goes first, and without it the subscription ranks last.

603.content: With the default `Priority` strategy, a worker with a topic subscription ranked 1 and a queue without a rank takes the payloads first. If the two have the same rank, the one bound first goes first. Strategies covers what priority does under the other three.

605.content: Block until a worker goes idle, pauses or stops, or until one job finishes.

611.content: `Add` returns at once, and the worker runs the job later. A set of calls on the worker block until the worker as a whole reaches a point: drained, paused or stopped. They do not wait for one job. For that, use the job's own handle (waiting on a job).

612.content: The scene below puts the wait calls of this page on one timeline. Pick a case, then press the button to let a blocked call go.

613.content: `Wait` and `WaitUntilIdle` both wait for the worker to finish its work. They differ in what they ask of the worker's status:

614.content:
| Worker's status     | `Wait` returns when                   | `WaitUntilIdle` returns when       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `Running` or `Idle` | no job is pending and none is running | the same, and the status is `Idle` |

615.content:
| Worker's status                              | `Wait` returns when                               | `WaitUntilIdle` returns when                     |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `Pausing`, `Paused`, `Stopping` or `Stopped` | no job is running, even if jobs are still pending | the worker is `Idle` again, with nothing pending |

616.content:
| Worker's status | `Wait` returns when              | `WaitUntilIdle` returns when            |
| --------------- | -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `Initiated`     | at once, even if jobs are queued | the worker has been started and drained |

618.content: On a worker that keeps running, both return when it has drained.

619.content: If something may pause or stop the worker, `Wait` returns when the running jobs have finished, and jobs that have not started stay queued. `WaitUntilIdle` keeps waiting through a pause or a stop, until a later `Resume`, `Restart` or `Start` brings the worker back to `Idle` and it drains.

620.content: A worker created with `WithAutoRun(false)` is `Initiated` until you call `Start`. `Wait` on it returns at once, with every job still queued. Start the worker first.

621.content: The program below pauses a worker while job 1 runs, with two more jobs queued behind it.

622.content: `Wait` returns once job 1 is done, while `NumProcessing` is 0 and `NumPending` is still 2. `WaitUntilIdle` keeps waiting through the pause. It returns only after `Resume` has let jobs 2 and 3 run.

623.content: Both cover everything bound to the worker: each queue and each topic subscription. They return at a moment when the worker is empty, so a job added afterwards is not waited for.

624.content: Do not call `Wait`, `WaitUntilIdle` or the combined calls below on a worker from inside that worker's own function. The job that is calling counts as running, so the call waits for the job it is in.

625.content: `Wait` and the other wait calls take no context and no timeout. To give up after a time, run the call in a goroutine and select on it:

626.content: The goroutine keeps waiting after the timeout. It ends when the worker drains, pauses or stops. Each call that times out leaves one goroutine waiting, so do not retry the timeout in a loop while the worker stays busy. When `Wait` returns, check `NumPending` and the status before you assume every job ran.

627.content: `WaitUntilPaused` and `WaitUntilStopped` wait for one status and look at nothing else. They return at once if the worker is already there. Otherwise they keep waiting until something puts it there, so a worker that you stop while you wait for `Paused` leaves the call waiting.

628.content: `Pause` and `Stop` return as soon as the change has started. While a job is running, the worker is `Pausing` or `Stopping`. Call `WaitUntilPaused` or `WaitUntilStopped` after them to wait until the change is over. The lifecycle page lists the states. Its first program shows a worker go from `Pausing` to `Paused`.

629.content: Four calls join a wait and a pause or a stop. The verb that comes first happens first.

630.content:
| Call           | Does                 | Returns when                                                |
| -------------- | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `WaitAndPause` | `Wait`, then `Pause` | `Pause` has been called. The worker can still be `Pausing`. |

631.content:
| Call           | Does                            | Returns when           |
| -------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `PauseAndWait` | `Pause`, then `WaitUntilPaused` | the worker is `Paused` |

632.content:
| Call          | Does                | Returns when                                                |
| ------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `WaitAndStop` | `Wait`, then `Stop` | `Stop` has been called. The worker can still be `Stopping`. |

633.content:
| Call          | Does                            | Returns when            |
| ------------- | ------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `StopAndWait` | `Stop`, then `WaitUntilStopped` | the worker is `Stopped` |

634.content: Each returns an `error`: the one `Pause` or `Stop` returns. `PauseAndWait` and `StopAndWait` return it without waiting when the pause or stop failed. The lifecycle page lists the errors.

635.content: **`WaitAndStop` drains, `StopAndWait` does not.** On a worker that is running, `WaitAndStop` lets every pending job run, then starts the stop. A job added after `Wait` returns can still be left queued. So stop adding jobs before you call it. On a paused worker, `Wait` returns with jobs still pending, and they stay queued. It returns before the worker has reached `Stopped`, so call `WaitUntilStopped` after it if you need that. `StopAndWait` starts the stop at once and blocks until the worker is `Stopped`. Running jobs finish, and jobs that had not started stay queued: `NumPending` counts them, and they run after a `Restart`. See what happens to jobs.

636.content: The program below gives two workers three jobs each. The first gets `StopAndWait` while job 1 runs, and the second gets `WaitAndStop`, followed by `WaitUntilStopped`.

637.content: Under `StopAndWait`, job 1 finishes and jobs 2 and 3 stay pending. Under `WaitAndStop`, all three jobs run before the worker stops.

638.content: The pause pair works the same way. `WaitAndPause` lets the work finish before it pauses. `PauseAndWait` pauses at once and waits for the running jobs to end.

639.content: Two methods on `Worker` count the work in flight:

640.content: `NumPending` is the number of jobs that have not started. It counts the jobs waiting in the bound queues and the jobs a goroutine has taken into a batch but not started. It also counts the jobs parked by a pause or stop. A queue's own `Len()` counts only the first group. A job you closed while it waited still counts until the worker reaches it. While a goroutine works through a batch, the batch's finished jobs still count until the whole batch ends. So during a run, it can be too high. It is exact once the worker is idle, paused or stopped.

641.content: `NumProcessing` is the number of jobs running right now. It is at most the concurrency limit, except for a while after `TunePool` lowers it.

642.content: Each is read on its own, so the two together are not a snapshot of one moment. They suit a progress display or a backpressure check. To know that the work is finished, use `Wait`. For counters over the worker's lifetime, see metrics.

644.content: NewWorker, NewErrWorker and NewResultWorker compared: what each returns, what Add gives back, and which queues each can bind.

649.content: Which queues each worker can bind

651.content: VarMQ has three worker constructors. In each, your worker function receives a `Job[T]`, where `T` is the type of the data you pass to `Add`. They differ in what the function returns. That decides what `Add` hands back, and how you find out what happened to a job.

652.content:
| Constructor | Your function    | `Add` returns | Read the outcome with |
| ----------- | ---------------- | ------------- | --------------------- |
| `NewWorker` | `func(j Job[T])` | `EnqueuedJob` | nothing to read       |

653.content:
| Constructor    | Your function          | `Add` returns    | Read the outcome with |
| -------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------- | --------------------- |
| `NewErrWorker` | `func(j Job[T]) error` | `EnqueuedErrJob` | `Err() error`         |

654.content:
| Constructor       | Your function               | `Add` returns          | Read the outcome with |
| ----------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------- |
| `NewResultWorker` | `func(j Job[T]) (R, error)` | `EnqueuedResultJob[R]` | `Result() (R, error)` |

655.content: Pick a constructor and a job below. The same function runs under all three, so you see what changes: the type `Add` hands back, and where a failure appears.

656.content: `R` is the type of the result. `Add` returns the handle together with a `bool`, `false` when the queue did not take the job. Jobs covers both.

657.content: `NewWorker` is for work that has nothing to report back. The handle lets you `Wait` for the job, read its status or close it while it waits, but it carries no outcome.

658.content: The worker's function prints `worker got hello`. `Wait` returns once the job is done, and there is nothing else to read from the handle.

659.content: If the function panics, the worker recovers and counts the job as failed. It reports the panic on the worker's `Errs()` channel and to the handler you set with `WithErrHandler`. The handle does not get it. Errors covers both.

660.content: `NewErrWorker` takes a function that returns an `error`. `Err()` blocks until the job is closed, then returns what the function returned: `nil` when it succeeded. A panic comes back through `Err()` as an error. The worker reports the same error on its own `Errs()` channel and to its error handler too, so one failure appears in both places.

661.content: A job that was closed before it ran also releases `Err`, with `nil`. So `nil` means the function reported no error, not that it ran. See closing a queued job.

662.content: `Err` returned what the function returned for each job: `<nil>` for 2 and `3 is odd` for 3. The program reads each outcome right after `Add` to stay short. In a real program you usually add many jobs first and read the outcomes later.

663.content: `NewResultWorker` takes a function that returns `(R, error)`. `Result()` blocks until the job is closed, then returns both.

664.content: When the function returns a non-nil error, `Result` returns that error and the zero value of `R`, whatever value the function returned beside it. A panic does the same: the zero value, and the panic as the error. As with an error worker, the error also reaches `Errs()` and the error handler.

665.content: `"42"` gives the result 42 and no error. `"forty-two"` gives the zero value of `int` and the error from `strconv.Atoi`.

666.content: Every handle has `ID()`, `Status()`, `IsClosed()`, `Wait()` and `Close()`. The error and result handles add `Err()` or `Result()`, and a `Drain()` method.

667.content: `Drain` does nothing on a single job. It exists for the group handles that `AddAll` returns (adding many jobs). So `Err` and `Result` give the same answer whether or not you call it.

668.content: Each constructor returns a binder that holds the binding methods: `IWorkerBinder[T]` from `NewWorker`, `IErrWorkerBinder[T]` from `NewErrWorker` and `IResultWorkerBinder[T, R]` from `NewResultWorker`. The in-memory binding methods return a queue handle whose type follows the worker.

673.content: An error or result worker binds in-memory queues only. For a persistent queue, a distributed queue or a topic, use `NewWorker`.

674.content: The handles in this guide are what an in-memory queue's `Add` returns. On a persistent or distributed queue, `Add` returns only a `bool`, `false` when the storage refused the job. There is no job handle, so there is nothing to `Wait` on or to read an outcome from.

675.content: All three constructors take the same trailing arguments, `config ...any`: an `int` for the concurrency, a `string` for the name, and option functions such as `WithAutoRun`. Configuration has the rules.

751.content: **A stopped worker stays for a while.** After it reaches `Stopped`, the `WithStoppedRetention` time starts. The default is one minute. When that time has passed, the worker is removed from the registry, unless it was started again. Lifecycle has the details.

| 409    | the call returned `ErrRunningWorker`, `ErrNotRunningWorker` or `ErrSameConcurrency` | `start` on a running worker, or a concurrency change to the same number | the error's message, for example `{"error":"worker is already running"}` |

773.content:
| Status | When                              | Example                                                                                                                                    | Body                                                             |
| ------ | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 500    | the call returned any other error | `ErrWorkerPausing`, `ErrWorkerPaused`, `ErrWorkerStopping` or `ErrWorkerStopped`: `resume` on a `Pausing` worker, `pause` on a stopped one | the error's message, for example `{"error":"worker is stopped"}` |

774.content: The last two rows follow the error the worker returns. `start` on a worker that is running, and a concurrency change to the number it already has, are 409. A worker that is `Pausing`, `Paused`, `Stopping` or `Stopped` answers some calls with `ErrWorkerPausing`, `ErrWorkerPaused`, `ErrWorkerStopping` or `ErrWorkerStopped`, and those are 500. So `resume` on a worker that is `Pausing` is a 500 with `worker is pausing`, and so is `pause` on a stopped one. Errors lists which call returns which error.

775.content: Two replies do not come from the routes. A path the mux does not know gets a plain-text `404 page not found`. A known path with the wrong method gets a plain-text `405 Method Not Allowed` with an `Allow` header.

776.content: `InstanceHeader` is the name of a response header, `X-Varmq-Instance`. Its value is `InstanceID`. When several instances sit behind one URL, such as a load balancer, the header tells you which process answered.

777.content: `InstanceID` is a package variable. It starts as the host name, which on Kubernetes is the pod name, or as an empty string if the host name is not available. Set it before you start serving when several instances share a host:

778.content: Every response from the routes carries the header, whether you use `Handler` or `NewServerMux`. As described above, only `Handler` also adds it to the mux's own 404 and 405 replies.

780.content: Common problems with VarMQ workers and queues, what causes each one, and what to do about it.

785.content: A job ran twice on Redis or SQLite

789.content: A job does not stop when the worker stops

790.content: The REST API does not list a worker

791.content: Each section below starts from what you see. It gives the usual causes, what to do, and the page with the details.

792.content: `Add` returns a `nil` handle and `false` in three cases, and it does not say which one. The queue is full, the queue is closed, or an in-memory queue already holds a job with the same ID.

793.content: Check `IsFull()` if you set `WithQueueCapacity`. Treat a full queue as backpressure: try again later, drop the job, or slow down the caller.

794.content: Look for a call to `Close` on the queue. A closed queue stays closed.

795.content: Look for a repeated `WithJobId`. The ID is free again once its job has left the queue.

797.content: A worker created with `WithAutoRun(false)` stays `Initiated` until you call `Start`. A paused or stopped worker does not start new jobs either, but `Add` still accepts them. Call `Start`, `Resume` or `Restart`, as the worker's status needs. The lifecycle page has the states.

798.content: `Wait` on an `Initiated` worker returns at once, with every job still queued. So the program can exit before any job runs. Start the worker before you call `Wait`. See waiting.

799.content: With your own persistent queue, old jobs can stay in storage if the worker started before you bound the queue. Create the worker with `WithAutoRun(false)`, bind the queue, then call `Start`. redisq and sqliteq signal the worker when you bind them, so with them the order does not matter. See starting a worker on a non-empty queue.

800.content: **You called it from inside the worker's own function.** The calling job counts as running, so the call waits for itself. Call it from outside the worker.

801.content: **The worker is paused or stopped.** `WaitUntilIdle` waits until the worker is `Idle` again with nothing pending. Call `Resume` or `Restart`.

802.content: **You wait for a state the worker does not reach.** `WaitUntilPaused` keeps waiting if the worker is stopped instead.

804.content: A queue has no limit by default, so jobs wait in memory when you add them faster than the worker runs them. Set `WithQueueCapacity` and handle a `false` from `Add`. See queues.

805.content: A topic subscriber that is slow, paused or stopped keeps every payload it has not read. Set `WithTopicCapacity`, or unsubscribe a worker that will not read again. See topics.

806.content: With redisq and sqliteq, the best case is at-least-once delivery. A job that was taken and not acknowledged runs again. Write the job function so that it is safe to run twice. Then check these causes:

807.content: **redisq:** a job ran longer than the visibility timeout, five minutes by default. Keep the timeout longer than your slowest job.

808.content: **sqliteq:** a second process opened a queue on the same database file. Use one process for each file.

809.content: **redisq:** the queue was closed while a job still ran. `Close` puts back every job that the queue object took and did not acknowledge. Call `StopAndWait` on the worker before you close the queue.

810.content: See what this guarantees, Redis and SQLite.

811.content: With concurrency above 1, jobs run at the same time and finish in any order. A goroutine can also take several jobs as a batch, so a later job on another goroutine can start first. If the order matters, use concurrency 1 and one FIFO queue. See batched dispatch.

812.content: A priority queue runs the lowest number first. A worker bound to several queues picks a queue for each job with its strategy. See queues and strategies.

813.content: `ErrSameConcurrency` means the worker already has that limit, so nothing changed. Any other error means the worker is not `Idle` or `Running`, and the error names its state. Call `TunePool` on an active worker only. See concurrency.

814.content: These errors come from the storage, not from your function. The worker sends them to `Errs()` and the error handler, and continues.

815.content: `ErrParseJob`: the stored bytes do not decode as JSON into the worker's job type. Make sure the producers and the consumers use the same type.

816.content: `ErrAcknowledgeJob`: the storage refused the acknowledgement. The job's function has already run. Check that the storage is reachable, and that nothing purged or closed the queue during the job.

817.content: `ErrFailedToDequeue`: the queue was not empty when the worker checked, but it gave no job when the worker pulled. If other workers or processes share the queue, one of them can take the last job between the check and the pull. Otherwise, check that the storage is reachable. With redisq or sqliteq as the worker's only queue, a failed storage call sends the storage's own error instead.

819.content: VarMQ does not interrupt a running function. `Stop` and a cancelled context only keep waiting jobs from starting. To end a job early, pass the worker's `Context()` to your calls, or select on its `Done` channel. See stopping a running job early.

820.content: Only a named worker is in the registry. Give the worker a name with `WithName`. A worker joins the registry when it starts, and leaves some time after it stops, one minute by default. See which workers it serves.

If an interface is not implemented, its behaviour is off. This is not an error. This page lists them all, from `IBaseQueue` to the small job interfaces. They are all in the `varmq` package.
